How I turned a Raspberry Pi into a Pi-based router and portable network console At the start of the year, I ended up with a Raspberry Pi and decided to use it as a way to grow my homelab and networking skills. Instead of dedicating it to a single task, I wanted to see how far I could push it as a small, multi-purpose system that actually supports the rest of my network. Before touching Pi-hole or routing, I started with monitoring. I set up a lightweight VNC server on the Pi and paired it with an old Samsung tablet I had lying around. Using F-Droid, I installed a VNC client and turned the tablet into a portable network console I could carry anywhere within my WLAN. On the Pi side, I kept things minimal, a simple desktop environment and URXVT as my terminal, which I use to access and monitor the Pi and my other servers(see image). Once that was stable, I moved on to the main goal: building a Pi-based router with a Pi-hole filtered Wi-Fi subnet. I’m running DietPi, and an early decision came back to matter later: the image I chose didn’t include everything needed to use the Pi’s internal Wi-Fi hardware the way I originally thought. Rather than changing operating systems, I opted to add USB Wi-Fi adapters, which also gave me clearer separation between interfaces and more capabilities. For now, the Pi uses Ethernet as its upstream connection, with Wi-Fi handling the filtered subnet. From there, the setup came together using Pi-hole for DNS filtering, hostapd for the Wi-Fi access point, dnsmasq scoped to the Wi-Fi interface for DHCP, and iptables for NAT and forwarding. The result is a clean split: my normal LAN remains untouched, while Wi-Fi clients connect to an isolated subnet where all traffic is filtered. I also added a small Ethernet switch to keep future expansion open. One issue I’ve noticed over time is that after running for extended periods, the router sometimes stops accepting new Wi-Fi clients until it’s restarted. Based on my research so far, this may be related to RF noise and USB Wi-Fi adapter behavior in a dense wireless environment, where connected devices are prioritized over discovery. It’s something I’m still investigating. Overall, this project ended up being less about ad blocking and more about understanding how routing, DHCP, DNS, and hardware decisions interact in real-world conditions. If anyone’s interested in building something similar or wants to talk through the approach, feel free to reach out to me here on LinkedIn. #RaspberryPi #Homelab #Networking #PiHole #Linux #LearningByDoing
